paras: The Armourdale mob chase and drowning took place on September 4, 1903, at Armourdale, Kansas, a suburb of Kansas City, when an unidentified Black man accused of choking a white widow, Margaret Gerahn, in her home was chased to the Kansas River by a crowd and drowned himself. According to the wire reports, he dived from a rowboat in midstream "rather than run the chances of being lynched," and his body was not recovered. The dispatch ran nationwide under headlines about escaping a mob, and the Montgomery Advertiser approved the outcome.

Gerahn was described as a 45-year-old widow whose husband, a packing-house employee, and son had drowned in "the great June flood," leaving her to live alone. The man was never named in the coverage; the Kansas versions of the dispatch gave his age as about 30.

By the fuller Kansas City account, the man came to Gerahn's house about noon, entered "stealthily," locked himself in, and demanded her money. When she said there was none in the house, he was reported to have threatened to kill her, choked her until she was unconscious, locked her in a closet, and later choked her repeatedly when she would not say where she kept her money. About three hours after he arrived, neighboring women broke into the house and found him standing over her with his fingers at her throat.

The man ran to the Kansas River, two blocks away according to the Wichita Daily Eagle, hired a boat, and ordered its owner to row quickly to the Missouri shore. When the boat reached midstream, a crowd of "excited men and boys" had gathered on the bank and shouted for it to return. As the boat turned back, he stood up, said "I have lived too long to die at the end of a rope," and dived into the water. He drowned before anyone could reach the spot, and his body disappeared.
Gerahn was reported seriously hurt but expected to recover. No report has the crowd catching or harming him, and no officers appear in the accounts.

A later version of the Kansas City dispatch, dated September 5, said the body had not yet been found. No report of the body's recovery, an inquest, the man's identity, or Gerahn's later condition was found in the coverage.

The story spread on September 5 in two differently worded Kansas City dispatches. A short version, printed by the Portland Daily Press and the Minneapolis Journal, said he was caught "in the act of assaulting" Gerahn and drowned himself when "escape was impossible." A longer version, printed by the St. Louis Republic, the Wichita Daily Eagle, the Topeka State Journal and the Salt Lake Herald, described a strangling during a demand for money.

Headlines centered on the mob and the rope: "Negro Drowned Himself. To Escape Lynching at Hands of An Angry Mob" in Portland, "He Foresaw Rope's End" in Wichita, and "Mob Was After the Miscreant" in Salt Lake City. Some headlines used "assault" even over the longer text, as the Omaha Daily Bee did with "Accused of Assaulting a Woman," while the Corvallis Times headed it an "Attempt to Rob Her." Weeklies that reprinted the story over the following week used harsher terms: the Watchman and Southron of Sumter, South Carolina, headed it "The Usual Crime in Kansas," and the Weekly Corinthian of Mississippi "Negro Fiend." A later version carried in Nebraska and South Dakota weeklies called the man "a black brute of thirty" and headed the story "Prospect of Lynching Bee."

The Montgomery Advertiser commented that the man "made a very satisfactory settlement of the matter but he deprived the Kansans of some congenial enjoyment." In the Black press the only item found was a single sentence in the Baltimore Afro-American's general news digest of September 12, which said he drowned himself "fearing that if caught he would be executed."

The short wire and several headlines called the attack an "assault," while the longer and more detailed dispatch described only choking to force Gerahn to give up money. On his motive, the white papers said lynching and the Afro-American's digest said execution.

bases: A crowd chased a Black man accused of choking a white woman to the river, where he drowned himself 'rather than run the chances of being lynched' (A3, A5); a threatened lynching, kept under the lynching type with stage 'threatened'.
A crowd of men and boys pursued him over an accusation (A3, A5), but he died by his own dive from a boat and no report has the crowd killing or harming him (A3).

Two differently worded Kansas City dispatches (A1, A3) and a later version (A31) agree on the choking, the crowd's chase and the drowning, though all come by wire from Kansas City and no local report was found.

accounts.label: Kansas City wire, long version
accounts.gist: The man held and repeatedly choked Gerahn for three hours demanding money, fled to the river and hired a boat; when a crowd on the bank shouted for its return he said he had 'lived too long to die at the end of a rope' and dived in.

accounts.label: Kansas City wire, short version
accounts.gist: He was caught 'in the act of assaulting' Gerahn, fled chased by a crowd, and drowned himself from a rowboat when escape was impossible; he had choked her for money over three hours.

accounts.label: Afro-American news digest
accounts.gist: A man who tried to strangle Gerahn escaped and drowned himself, fearing he would be executed if caught; no crowd mentioned.

framing.detail: Most papers printed the Kansas City wire as fact under mob-and-rope headlines ('To Escape Lynching at Hands of An Angry Mob', 'He Foresaw Rope's End').
Montgomery Advertiser called the drowning 'a very satisfactory settlement' that deprived Kansans of 'some congenial enjoyment'.
Reprinting weeklies sharpened the language: 'The Usual Crime in Kansas', 'Negro Fiend', 'a black brute of thirty', 'Prospect of Lynching Bee'.
Baltimore Afro-American gave one uncommented digest sentence, saying he feared execution rather than lynching.
